A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same prior-elicitation framework and study. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices support comparison despite extensive rewriting, reorganization, and replacement of some experiments.

before.justification: v1 reports original predictive-performance experiments, in-context model diagnostics, memorisation tests, and prompt-sensitivity analyses in the main text and appendices.

after.justification: v4 retains original empirical results and reports additional clinical-task and DeepSeek evaluations, including predictive performance and distributional comparisons.

M1.justification: AutoElicit names the existing method: Gaussian-mixture priors from 100 task descriptions, Bayesian linear/logistic prediction, MLE-based in-context parameter extraction, and Bayes-factor selection remain. Incorporating expert information into prompts was already demonstrated in v1 Section 3.2.

E1.justification: Wine Quality classification and California Housing regression are removed and replaced by Hypothyroid classification and Diabetes progression regression throughout the evaluations. UTI, Heart Disease, Breast Cancer, and the synthetic task remain. This substantially redirects real-world coverage toward clinical applications.

E2.justification: DeepSeek-R1-32B-Q4 priors join the evaluated alternatives. The open-source comparison also adds GPT-4-turbo priors alongside the retained GPT-3.5, Llama, Qwen, and uninformative priors (v1 Figure 17; v4 Figure 18). GPT-4, GPT-4o-mini, Llama, and Qwen evaluations themselves already existed in v1.

E3.justification: v4 introduces evaluation of a 32-billion-parameter DeepSeek model with 4-bit quantisation. The replacement datasets introduce a balanced 150-example Hypothyroid evaluation and Diabetes targets scaled to 0–10. The established 50/50 splits, participant-separated UTI evaluation, and posterior-sampling budgets remain.

E4.justification: Memorisation, prompt-count sensitivity, and in-context distribution diagnostics are revised for Hypothyroid and Diabetes, replacing Wine Quality and California Housing analyses. The UTI timing case study incorporates DeepSeek. The expert-information experiment, synthetic prompt-detail ablation, and model-class compliance test are retained rather than newly introduced.

E5.justification: v4 Appendix A.7.3 specifies 95% confidence intervals where v1 Appendix A.5.2 described standard deviations, aligning that passage with existing figure captions. Sampling descriptions are also clarified. Ten splits, five chains of 5,000 samples, and confidence intervals were already documented in v1; increased replication is not established.

E6.justification: v4 adds DeepSeek performance curves and replaces extensive Wine Quality/California Housing results with Hypothyroid/Diabetes results. New posterior energy statistics include 0.06 ± 0.01 and 0.02 ± 0.00, respectively (Table 4). The UTI timing illustration changes from approximately 200 to 220 days with DeepSeek added. v1 Figure 6's prior accuracy/MSE panels are removed; these changes do not establish a same-setting performance gain.

T1.justification: v1 Section 2.1 explicitly assumes equal probabilities for relevant task descriptions and zero probability for irrelevant descriptions. v4 defines the task-description distribution without retaining these explicit assumptions. The mixture, MLE, energy-statistic, and Bayes-factor mathematics otherwise remain substantially unchanged.

C1.justification: The central contributions remain prior elicitation, investigation of in-context inference, and model selection. v4 emphasizes interpretable clinical linear models, extends the concluding performance claim to DeepSeek alongside the OpenAI models, and updates the headline UTI timing example to approximately 220 days.

C2.justification: The interpretation of Heart Disease reverses: v1 Section 3.5 and Appendix A.8 treat its posterior agreement as evidence of approximate Bayesian inference, whereas v4 Section 5.6 treats it as a mismatch. The aggregate energy statistic remains 0.04 ± 0.01, and the illustrated single-split value remains 0.032. This materially changes the reliability interpretation. v4 also adds reasoning/test-time-scaling explanations for DeepSeek performance and an A100 resource limitation.

D1.justification: v4 adds a callable elicitation-code example, documents LLM wrappers and ollama version 0.4.7, specifies the GPT-4 snapshot, and reports using an Nvidia A100 for DeepSeek. It also describes the UTI sensors more explicitly. The repository reference and most implementation and sampling details were already present.

R1.justification: v4 substantially expands positioning around human expert elicitation, automated modelling pipelines, and clinical interpretability. New discussion distinguishes the method from Gouk and Gao's synthetic-data approach and raises memorisation concerns. New clinical and elicitation references supplement the earlier background, much of which moves to Appendix A.2.

P1.justification: The paper is extensively rewritten and reorganized into separate Related Work, Background, Methods, and Results sections. Earlier background and model-selection discussion move into appendices, the question/method/finding introduction is replaced, and terminology shifts from 'truthfulness' toward 'consistency.' AutoElicit branding accompanies these broader narrative changes.

P2.justification: v4 adopts a two-column layout and substantially restructures the displays. Figure 1 combines the method schematic with the clinical timing illustration; performance histograms move into an expanded appendix figure; posterior comparisons become prominent main-text plots; and the posterior-statistics table moves to the appendix. Legends, dataset grids, captions, and histogram scales are revised.

improvement.justification: v4 improves clarity and practical usability through better-separated exposition, fuller research positioning, a code example, and DeepSeek evaluations with explicit hardware requirements. The replacement clinical tasks strengthen the clinical application while narrowing domain coverage. These gains are limited by the insufficiently explained reversal of the Heart Disease Bayesian-inference interpretation despite unchanged energy statistics; the revision does not establish a substantial overall scientific improvement.
